Guru Gobind Singh

Stories of the Sikh Gurus

Guru Gobind Singh

The Guru of the Khalsa

In everyday English — the whole story of the tenth Guru

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the air of the Anandpur hills and the sound of kirtan in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Gobind Singh's bold and clear, Tegh Bahadur's calm and grave, and nine-year-old Gobind's fearless.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader, not the listener.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are three kinds of things in this book — the Guru's own bani, written in the Dasam Granth and the Zafarnama; the stories of the tradition, told in the sangat for centuries; and the writings of people of that time, like the Emperor's letters. Where a story comes from the tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where a thing is certain, the book names it.

This book's main story comes from the Janamsakhis, Gurbilas literature, the Dasam Granth, and the checking of modern scholars. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Guru Gobind Singh — the heart of this story. Gobind Rai as a boy, the tenth Guru at nine years old, the Guru of the Khalsa, a poet and a warrior — the saint-soldier.

Guru Tegh Bahadur — Gobind Singh's father, the ninth Guru of the Sikhs. Hind di Chadar, the Shield of India — who gave his life in Delhi so that no one else would have to fear for their faith.

Mata Gujri — Gobind Singh's mother, the wife of Tegh Bahadur.

Mata Sundari — Gobind Singh's wife.

Mata Sahib Kaur — called the Mother of the Khalsa in the tradition — who added the patashas, the sugar crystals, to the amrit.

The four Sahibzade — the Guru's four sons: Ajit Singh (18), Jujhar Singh (14), Zorawar Singh (9) and Fateh Singh (7).

The Panj Pyare — the first five Sikhs of the Khalsa: Daya Singh, Dharam Singh, Himmat Singh, Mohkam Singh and Sahib Singh.

Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh — two of the Panj Pyare, who carried the Zafarnama to Aurangzeb.

Bhai Mani Singh — the Guru's learned companion, who the tradition tells us helped write the Granth at Damdama Sahib.

Bhai Jaita — the Sikh who, the tradition tells us, brought Tegh Bahadur's head from Delhi to Anandpur.

Aurangzeb — the Emperor of India, by whose order Tegh Bahadur was killed, and to whom the Guru wrote the Zafarnama.

Wazir Khan — the governor of Sirhind, to whom the younger Sahibzade were handed over, the tradition tells us.

Banda Singh Bahadur — the Bairagi who met the Guru at Nanded, and whom the Guru sent to Punjab.

1 · Birth — Patna · · BIRTH — PATNA

On the banks of the river Ganga, far to the east, there was an old city — Patna. There, in the year 1666, on 5 January 1666, a child was born. His name was Gobind Rai. His father was Guru Tegh Bahadur — the ninth Guru of the Sikhs — and his mother was Mata Gujri.

Gobind Rai's father was not at home then — he was on a long journey to the east, as far as Bengal and Assam. The child was born in Patna, and the sangat celebrated — a son had come to the Guru's house.

The tradition tells us that at the child's birth in Patna, a faqir came — Bhikhan Shah — who looked at the baby and said — this child will grow up to do a very great work. The sangat took his words to heart.

Even as a child, Gobind Rai was different from the others. The tradition tells us that from childhood he loved horse-riding and the bow and arrow — and he listened to bani too. His mother Gujri told him stories — of Nanak, of Arjan, of Hargobind — and the child listened with shining eyes.

When Gobind Rai was five years old, the family came back from Patna to Punjab — to Anandpur — the same city his father had founded. Patna was left behind — but the memory of Patna stayed with the Guru all his life. Even today, that place stands in Patna — Takht Sri Harmandir Sahib, Patna Sahib — where the sangat remembers the Guru's birth.

The date of birth — 5 January 1666

Gobind Rai was born on 5 January 1666 in Patna — this date is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, and it is the same date used in the earlier books of this series. He was the son of Guru Tegh Bahadur and Mata Gujri.

Bhikhan Shah — the tradition's story

The coming of the faqir Bhikhan Shah to Patna, and his great words on seeing the child, is the tradition's story — told in the Janamsakhis and Gurbilas literature. This book tells it as the tradition's story.

Pause and think — Gobind Rai was born in Patna — far from Punjab, on the banks of the Ganga. Do you think a person is who they are because of where they were born — or because of what they become when they grow up?

2 · The Nine-Year-Old Guru — 1675 · · THE NINE-YEAR-OLD GURU — 1675

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

The year 1675 came. Gobind Rai was nine years old. He lived in Anandpur — study, play, and bani — all together. Then one day came news no one had expected — his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, had been killed in Delhi.

The tradition tells us that Tegh Bahadur had gone to Delhi to protect people who were being forced to give up their faith — and he had said to the Emperor — change me first. The Emperor had him killed. The full story of his martyrdom is in the previous book (Guru Tegh Bahadur) — here there is only as much as is needed to understand Gobind's story.

The tradition tells us that Tegh Bahadur's head was brought by Bhai Jaita from Delhi to Anandpur — through storm and rain, walking night after night. In Anandpur the last rites were held — and the sangat bid farewell to its Guru, weeping.

Mata Gujri held her nine-year-old son close. Gobind Rai saw — his father, who was so calm, who sat in meditation, was no more. And he had gone only because he had stood up to protect someone else's faith.

The sangat looked at Gobind Rai — and understood. The guruship would come to him. In 1675, at nine years old, Gobind Rai became the tenth Guru of the Sikhs — Guru Gobind Singh.

Gobind Singh understood — his father had taught one thing by giving his life — fear no one, and frighten no one. That became his life — and later, the foundation of the Khalsa too.

The certain part of the martyrdom — what is proved

The certain part of the martyrdom is this — Guru Tegh Bahadur was killed in November 1675 in Delhi's Chandni Chowk — by the order of Emperor Aurangzeb, for standing firm on his faith. The date differs between sources — the Sikh tradition marks the martyrdom on 24 November 1675, some sources give 11 November — as in the previous book.

Bhai Jaita and the head — the tradition's story

Bhai Jaita bringing Tegh Bahadur's head from Delhi to Anandpur is the tradition's story — told in the Gurbilas literature. There is no contemporary record of it. This book tells it as the tradition's story.

Pause and think — Gobind was only nine years old when his father was gone — and the whole sangat's responsibility fell on him. Do you think a difficult time breaks a person — or makes them stronger? And is it right to give your life to protect someone else's faith?

3 · The Years at Anandpur — Poet and Warrior · · THE YEARS AT ANANDPUR — POET AND WARRIOR

Gobind Singh grew up in Anandpur Sahib — near the Shivalik hills, on the banks of the Sutlej river, the same city his father had founded under the name Chakk Nanaki. Anandpur was his home, his school, and his court too.

In Anandpur, Gobind Singh learned everything — the languages Punjabi, Persian, Sanskrit and Braj; horse-riding, archery and swordsmanship; and with it all, bani — his grandfather Hargobind's Miri-Piri, and his father's calm. In the morning he did kirtan, and in the day he practised in the field.

Gobind Singh was also a poet — and a great poet. He composed Jaap Sahib — the bani of God's praise, still read every morning today. He composed Akal Ustat — and wrote his life story in Bachittar Natak — who he was, where he had come from, and why he had become Guru. His bani is in the Dasam Granth today.

The tradition tells us that fifty-two poets lived in the court at Anandpur — learned men come from far away, who recited their poetry before the Guru. The Guru gave them gifts — and said — poetry too is a sword, one that touches the heart.

But Gobind Singh was not only a poet — he was a warrior too. In 1688, at Bhangani, the first battle was fought — the army of the hill rajas had come, and the Guru's army pushed it back. That was the Guru's first battle — and he wrote it himself in his story, Bachittar Natak.

In Anandpur the Guru taught the sangat one more thing — that a poet and a warrior can live in the same person. The one who writes bani can also take up the sword — and the one who takes up the sword can also write bani. Hargobind had spoken of Miri-Piri — Gobind Singh lived it in his own life.

Fifty-two poets — the tradition's story

The fifty-two poets living in the court at Anandpur is the tradition's telling — told in the Gurbilas literature. It is certain that poets and scholars lived in Gobind Singh's court — their number is what the tradition gives.

The Dasam Granth — what is certain, what is debated

Guru Gobind Singh's bani — Jaap Sahib, Akal Ustat, Bachittar Natak, Chandi Charitar, the Zafarnama — is found in the Dasam Granth. But scholars debate the authorship of the whole Dasam Granth — some hold that the entire Granth is the Guru's own writing, others hold that it also contains the work of court poets. This book calls only those works the Guru's which are generally held to be his — and the debate is recorded here.

The battle of Bhangani — 1688

The battle of Bhangani was fought in 1688 — the Guru's first battle, against the hill rajas. The Guru wrote it himself in his story Bachittar Natak — so this battle is known from the Guru's own witness. The details of the battle are what the tradition tells.

Pause and think — In the morning Gobind Singh wrote poetry, and in the day he wielded the sword. Do you think poetry and the sword can live together? And can one person hold both — gentleness and strength — at the same time?

4 · The Khalsa — Baisakhi 1699 · · THE KHALSA — BAISAKHI 1699

Then came the day that changed Sikh dharma for ever — Baisakhi, 13 April 1699, Anandpur Sahib. The sangat had come from far and wide — thousands of people, seated in the field. Guru Gobind Singh came onto the stage — a bare sword in his hand — and said —

Gobind Singh: I need one head. Who will give me their head? (In a loud, ringing voice)

Silence fell over the sangat. No one stood up. The Guru said again — I need one head. Still no one stood up. The Guru said it a third time — and then one man stood up — Daya Singh, from Lahore. The Guru took him inside the tent.

Then the Guru came out — blood on the sword — and said — I need one more head. A second man stood up — Dharam Singh. Then a third — Himmat Singh. Then a fourth — Mohkam Singh. Then a fifth — Sahib Singh. The Guru took all five, one by one, inside the tent — and all five came back alive.

The Guru called those five the Panj Pyare — the five beloved ones. Then he gave them amrit to drink — sweetened water, prepared with a khanda, a double-edged sword, in an iron bowl. The tradition tells us that Mata Sahib Kaur had mixed patashas, sugar crystals, into that water — so that the amrit would have sweetness in it as well as strength.

Then the Guru himself took amrit from those same five — and said — from today you are the Khalsa — the pure, the ones who belong to God. And from today my name too has changed — I am now Gobind Singh — and you are all Singh too — lions. Every Sikh woman's name will be Kaur — princess.

The Khalsa's five marks were made — Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kirpan, Kachhera — the five 'K's. Kesh — the tied hair; Kangha — the comb, to keep the hair tidy; Kara — the iron bangle, on the wrist; Kirpan — the small sword, at the waist; Kachhera — the soldier's dress. These five marks became the Khalsa's identity — they are seen, and they remind.

And one greeting was made — still heard in every gurdwara today — Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh — God's Khalsa, God's victory. The tradition tells us that this greeting began on the day of the Khalsa.

The Khalsa was not only a new identity — it was a new promise. The Khalsa will fear no one — and frighten no one. The Khalsa will protect the poor, and stand up before tyranny. The Guru said — from today the sangat itself is the Guru, and the Guru is the sangat.

The founding of the Khalsa — what is certain

The founding of the Khalsa — Baisakhi 1699, Anandpur Sahib, the Panj Pyare — is certain, and the strongest witness of the Sikh tradition. The names of the Panj Pyare — Daya Singh, Dharam Singh, Himmat Singh, Mohkam Singh, Sahib Singh — are held as certain in the tradition. The five 'K's and the names Singh and Kaur are also certain as the Khalsa's identity.

The amrit and the tent — the tradition's story

The details of preparing the amrit — the iron bowl, the khanda, the sweetened water — and what happened inside the tent are the tradition's story. This book says nothing of what happened inside the tent — only that all five came back alive and were called the Panj Pyare. The Guru taking amrit from the Panj Pyare himself is also recorded in the tradition.

Mata Sahib Kaur and the patashas — the tradition's story

Mata Sahib Kaur mixing patashas into the amrit is the tradition's story — which is why the tradition calls her the Mother of the Khalsa. This book tells it as the tradition's story.

The Khalsa greeting — the tradition's telling

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh — this greeting, the tradition holds, began on the day of the Khalsa. That is the tradition's telling — and today this greeting is every Sikh's identity.

Pause and think — Gobind Singh said — from today you are the Khalsa. Can a name — Singh, Kaur — change a person? And does your name ask anything of you? And the five marks — can a mark remind a person of who they are?

5 · The Siege of Anandpur and Chamkaur — 1704 · · THE SIEGE OF ANANDPUR AND CHAMKAUR — 1704

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

After the Khalsa, the sangat at Anandpur grew even more — and fear grew in the Emperor's court too. The hill rajas asked Aurangzeb for help — and from the year 1700, the siege of Anandpur began.

In 1704 the siege was at its longest — for months Anandpur was surrounded. The sangat's food ran out, the water ran out. Then an oath was sworn from the Emperor's side — a hand on the Quran, a promise — leave Anandpur, and you will be allowed to go in safety. The Guru trusted it — and in December 1704 he left Anandpur.

But the promise was broken. On the way itself — on the banks of the Sarsa river — the army attacked. The Guru's family was separated — Mata Gujri and the younger sons were left on one side, the Guru and the elder sons on the other.

The Guru reached Chamkaur with his forty companions — a small mud fort, a garhi. There, in December 1704, a battle was fought. The Guru's two elder sons — Ajit Singh, eighteen years old, and Jujhar Singh, fourteen years old — were killed in that battle.

The Guru had lost both his sons — and still he stood firm. The tradition tells us he said — my sons are gone, but the Khalsa still lives. And the Guru slipped out of Chamkaur in the dark of night — onto the road ahead.

The siege and the promise — what is certain

The siege of Anandpur, leaving Anandpur in December 1704, and the breaking of the promise sworn on the Quran — this is certain, because the Guru wrote it himself in his letter, the Zafarnama. The family's separation on the banks of the Sarsa river is recorded in both tradition and history.

Chamkaur — the date and the certain part

The battle of Chamkaur was fought on 21–22 December 1704 — this date is held in the sources. The Guru had forty companions with him in the battle — that too is in the Zafarnama. The details of the battle — who fought when, and how — are the tradition's story, and this book writes no detail.

The elder Sahibzade — the tradition's story, a certain heart

The elder Sahibzade — Ajit Singh (18) and Jujhar Singh (14) — being killed at Chamkaur is the tradition's story, with a certain heart — that both died in 1704 is held to be true. This book tells their martyrdom in a single line, from afar, with no detail — and no picture of them has been made.

Pause and think — The Guru trusted a promise — and the promise was broken. Do you think trusting is the mistake — or is breaking trust the mistake? And why did the Guru not give up, even after losing both his sons?

6 · Sirhind — The Younger Sahibzade · · SIRHIND — THE YOUNGER SAHIBZADE

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

The family had been separated on the banks of the Sarsa river. Mata Gujri was left on one side with her two young grandsons — Zorawar Singh, nine years old, and Fateh Singh, seven years old. The tradition tells us they were taken to Sirhind — to the governor, Wazir Khan.

In Sirhind the two young sons were told — give up your faith. Both refused — a seven-year-old child and a nine-year-old child — both said, we will not give up our faith.

And then, in 1704–05, both the younger Sahibzade were killed in Sirhind. Their grandmother, Mata Gujri, also passed away in those same days — in grief for her grandsons.

Guru Gobind Singh had lost all four of his sons in a single month — and his mother too. The Sikh tradition calls them the four Sahibzade — and every year in December the sangat remembers them — in Shaheedi Saptah, the week of martyrdom, quietly, lighting lamps.

Nothing more than this is said in this part — and no picture of the younger Sahibzade has been made either.

The younger Sahibzade — the tradition's story, a certain heart

The younger Sahibzade — Zorawar Singh (9) and Fateh Singh (7) — being killed in Sirhind is the tradition's story, with a certain heart — that both died in 1704–05 is held to be true. The date differs between sources — some say December 1704, some January 1705 — so this book's main story says '1704–05'. The details of the deaths are what the tradition tells, and this book writes no detail.

Mata Gujri — the tradition's story

Mata Gujri being with her grandsons in Sirhind, and her death in those same days, is the tradition's story — told in the Gurbilas literature. This book tells it in a single line, from afar.

Pause and think — A seven-year-old child and a nine-year-old child — both refused to give up their faith. Do you think standing firm on the truth is only the work of grown-ups — or of children too? And why did the Guru not give up the Khalsa, even after losing all four sons?

7 · The Zafarnama — A Letter to the Emperor · · THE ZAFARNAMA — A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR

After Chamkaur the Guru moved toward Malwa — through the sandy plains, from village to village. On the way he gathered his companions again — and stopped in a village — Dina. There, in the year 1705, the Guru wrote a letter — the Zafarnama — the letter of victory.

The Zafarnama was a real letter — in Persian, in verse, in 111 stanzas — written to Emperor Aurangzeb. In it the Guru wrote — you swore an oath on the Quran, and you broke your promise. You promised safe passage from Anandpur — and had us attacked on the road.

In the letter the Guru said to the Emperor — I do not fear you. You killed my four sons — but the Khalsa still lives. And then he invited the Emperor to meet him — he said, come to Dina, I will do you no harm.

The most famous line of the Zafarnama is in a single verse — the Guru wrote —

Guru Gobind Singh: Chu kar az hameh heelate dar guzasht, halal ast burdan ba-shamsheer dast. — When all other means have failed, it is righteous to take the sword in hand. (Slowly, in a firm voice)

This line is the heart of the Khalsa — the sword is not the first choice, it is the last road. First talk, first promise, first try everything — and when everything has been tried, and still there is no justice — only then take up the sword.

The Guru sent this letter by the hands of Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh to Aurangzeb — who was then in the south, in Ahmednagar. The letter is in the Dasam Granth today — and the Sikhs hold it to be the Guru's own voice.

After Dina the Guru moved on — and reached Muktsar. There another battle was fought — and in it fought those forty Sikhs who had already left Anandpur. The tradition tells us that they gave back their letter of disavowal — the bedawa — to the Guru, and the Guru tore it up. Those forty are called the Chali Mukte today — the forty who were freed.

Then the Guru went to Damdama Sahib — Talwandi Sabo. The tradition tells us that there he added his father Tegh Bahadur's bani to the Adi Granth — and the Granth was completed. That same Granth later became the Guru Granth Sahib — whose story will come in the next book.

The Zafarnama — a real letter

The Zafarnama is a real letter — Guru Gobind Singh wrote it in Persian, in verse, and it is found in the Dasam Granth. It has 111 stanzas — praising God, telling of Chamkaur, complaining of the broken promise, and inviting the Emperor to meet. The letter was sent by the hands of Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh.

The date of the Zafarnama — 1705 or 1706?

The date of the Zafarnama differs a little between sources — most sources say 1705, some say 1706 too. The letter was written from Dina — some sources also name the nearby village of Kangar. This book's main story says '1705, Dina', and the difference is recorded here.

The sword verse — verse 22 of the Zafarnama

The famous sword verse — Chu kar az hameh heelate dar guzasht, halal ast burdan ba-shamsheer dast — is verse 22 of the Zafarnama. It means — when all other means have failed, it is righteous to take the sword in hand. This book tells this verse in Persian and with its English meaning, as the Guru's own voice.

The Chali Mukte — the tradition's story

The forty Sikhs fighting at Muktsar, and the tearing up of the bedawa, is the tradition's telling — told in the Gurbilas literature. The battle of Muktsar was fought in 1705 — that is held to be true. This book tells this story as the tradition's story.

The Granth at Damdama Sahib — the tradition's story

The Guru adding Tegh Bahadur's bani to the Adi Granth at Damdama Sahib — and Bhai Mani Singh writing it — is the tradition's story. This book tells it as the tradition's story — the full story of the Granth will come in the next book (Guru Granth Sahib).

Pause and think — The Guru wrote a letter to the Emperor — not in anger, but demanding justice. Do you think it is easy to speak the truth to a powerful man — or hard? And trying everything before taking up the sword — is that weakness, or the greatest strength?

8 · Nanded — Banda Singh Bahadur · · NANDED — BANDA SINGH BAHADUR

After Muktsar and Damdama the Guru moved south — and in the year 1708 he reached Nanded — on the banks of the Godavari river, in Maharashtra. There the Guru made his camp — and the sangat began to come.

In Nanded there lived a Bairagi — Madho Das. The tradition tells us that the Guru went to meet him — and when Madho Das saw the Guru, he understood — this is the true Guru. The Guru gave him a new name — Banda Singh Bahadur — and said — go to Punjab, and protect the sangat there.

The tradition tells us that the Guru gave Banda Singh five arrows, a drum and a banner — and sent five Singhs with him. Banda Singh went to Punjab — and there he won Sirhind — the same Sirhind where the younger Sahibzade had been killed.

The story of Banda Singh Bahadur does not end here — it is a story of its own, told separately in Sikh history. In this book there is only this much — the Guru chose a man in Nanded, and sent him to Punjab — because the Guru knew that the Khalsa would now have to protect itself.

The meeting with Banda Singh Bahadur — the tradition's story

The Guru meeting Madho Das in Nanded, giving him the name Banda Singh Bahadur, and sending him to Punjab with five arrows, a drum and a banner — all of this is the tradition's story, told in the Gurbilas literature. Banda Singh going to Punjab and winning Sirhind is recorded in history.

Pause and think — The Guru chose a Bairagi — and sent him to Punjab. Do you think the Guru should have looked at a man's birth or his past — or only at what he wants to do now?

9 · The Guruship Passes to the Granth — 1708 · · THE GURUSHIP PASSES TO THE GRANTH — 1708

In Nanded the Guru called the sangat. The sangat gathered — and the Guru said — now listen. Ten Gurus came — from Nanak to me — one light, ten lamps. Now that light will not go into any man — it will go into the Granth.

The Guru seated the Guru Granth Sahib on the throne — and said — from today this is the Guru. The bani itself is the Guru, the word itself is the Guru. Whatever you wish to ask the Guru, ask the Granth. Whatever you wish to hear from the Guru, hear it from the bani.

The tradition tells us the Guru said — Sab Sikhan ko hukam hai, Guru manio Granth — it is the order to all Sikhs — take the Granth as the Guru. And with it he said — the Khalsa itself is the Panth — the Khalsa is the sangat, the Khalsa is the form of the Guru.

In Nanded the Guru was attacked — and a few days later, on 7 October 1708, he passed away. He was forty-two years old — and had been Guru for thirty-three years.

After Guru Gobind Singh no eleventh Guru came — and that is the greatest thing in this story. The guruship did not go to any man — it went to the Granth. And the Khalsa — which had been adorned in 1699 — became the Panth itself.

Even today that place stands in Nanded — Takht Sri Hazur Sahib — where the Guru gave the guruship to the Granth. The sangat goes there — and sits before the Granth and hears the same words the Guru spoke — fear no one, and frighten no one.

The guruship to the Granth — what is certain

Guru Gobind Singh giving the guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib in 1708 at Nanded is certain, and the greatest witness of the Sikh tradition. After this no human Guru came — that is the foundation of the Sikh faith. The Guru passed away on 7 October 1708 at Nanded — this date is held in the sources.

'Guru manio Granth' — the tradition's words

'Sab Sikhan ko hukam hai, Guru manio Granth' — these words are held in the tradition to be the Guru's own words, and they are found in the Rahitnamas. There is no contemporary record of them — so this book tells them as the tradition's words.

Pause and think — Gobind Singh gave the guruship to a book — not to any man. Can a book be a Guru? And in your life, which book is there that you learn something from?

To Think About · · TO THINK ABOUT

The story of Gobind Singh is not the story of a king, not the story of a warrior. It is the story of a child who became Guru at nine years old — after his father's martyrdom — and who gave the Panth a new identity.

His message fits in a single line — when all other means have failed, it is righteous to take the sword in hand. First talk, first promise, first try everything — and when everything has been tried, and still there is no justice — only then take up the sword. The sword is not the first choice — it is the last road.

Gobind Singh taught that the name itself is the identity. Singh — lion. Kaur — princess. The five marks — they are seen, and they remind. The Khalsa will fear no one — and frighten no one.

And the greatest thing — Gobind Singh taught that a book too can be a Guru. He did not give the guruship to any man — he gave it to the Granth. Ten Gurus went — but the light did not go. As one lamp lights another lamp — the flame stays the same, the lamp changes. Nanak's flame still burns today — in the Granth, in the sangat, and in the langar's pangat.

Gobind Singh lost all four of his sons — and his mother too. Still he did not give up the Khalsa — and wrote in the Zafarnama — my four sons are gone, but the Khalsa still lives. That is the strength of the Khalsa — it does not live in one man, it lives in the sangat.

But this tenth book ends here — in Nanded, on the banks of the Godavari river, with a question — if Gobind Singh were here today, what would he say in your home, in your city? Perhaps this — remember the Name, share your food — and when anyone does wrong, stand up before them. And remember — the sword is the last road, not the first.

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main sources — Janamsakhis and Gurbilas

This book's main story comes from the Janamsakhis and Gurbilas literature — the stories of Gobind Singh's life are found in these. They were written decades and centuries after his death, and they hold both history and tradition. In this book every story of the tradition is told with 'the tradition tells us' and made clear in its own note.

The Guru's own bani — the Dasam Granth

Guru Gobind Singh's own bani is in the Dasam Granth — Jaap Sahib, Akal Ustat, Bachittar Natak, Chandi Charitar. His life story in Bachittar Natak is his own witness — the battle of Bhangani is known from there too. The debate among scholars over the authorship of the whole Dasam Granth is recorded in this book's third part.

The Zafarnama — a real letter

The Zafarnama is Guru Gobind Singh's real letter — in Persian, in verse, in 111 stanzas, written in 1705 from Dina, and sent by the hands of Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh to Aurangzeb. It is found in the Dasam Granth. In this book the sword verse (verse 22) is told in Persian and with its English meaning.

Chamkaur and Sirhind — what is certain, what is tradition

The heart of the deaths at Chamkaur and Sirhind is certain — all four Sahibzade died in 1704–05, that is held to be true. But the details of the battles — who fought when, how they fought, what happened in Sirhind — are the tradition's story, and this book writes no detail. Both martyrdoms are told in a single line each, from afar.

The Khalsa — what is certain, what is tradition

The founding of the Khalsa — Baisakhi 1699, Anandpur Sahib, the Panj Pyare — is certain. The details of the amrit, what happened inside the tent, Mata Sahib Kaur's patashas and the Khalsa greeting — these are the tradition's story, and this book tells them as the tradition's story.

The guruship to the Granth — 1708

Guru Gobind Singh giving the guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib in 1708 at Nanded is certain — after this no human Guru came. The words 'Guru manio Granth' are the tradition's, and are found in the Rahitnamas.

Modern scholarship

The dates and events of this book were checked against the work of modern scholars — J.S. Grewal, 'The Sikhs of the Punjab'; W.H. McLeod, 'The Sikhs — History, Religion and Society'; Max Arthur Macauliffe, 'The Sikh Religion'; and the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala). Where scholars and tradition say different things, both are recorded in the book.

One clear thing

In this book Guru Gobind Singh is not shown against any religion. His battles were with the Emperor's army — not with any faith. In the Khalsa there were Hindus too, and Muslims too. His message was not to divide, but to join — and to stand up against tyranny.

The End · · THE END

The story is complete — but Guru Gobind Singh's Khalsa is not yet over.

In the next book — Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal Guru — the Granth that holds the bani of the ten Gurus, and which is the Guru of the Sikhs even today.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh.
